hero.title: A language carries a way of thinking and living
hero.intro: These proverbs have crossed generations. They were shaped by great minds whose knowledge is still hard to measure.

questions.title: Five questions to understand
questions.intro: Speaking, studying and passing on a language keeps alive a mindset, a way of speaking and a way of life.

identity.label: Identity
identity.a1: The Mandé is a cultural area of West Africa around Mali, Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire, Senegal and Burkina Faso. Its related languages include Bambara, Dioula, Maninka, Malinke, Mandinka and Susu.
identity.a2: Speaking your language says who you are: greetings, storytelling and your place in a family and community all pass through words.

culture.label: Culture
culture.q: How do people in the Sahel live in mud-brick houses that last for centuries?
culture.a1: Banco is raw earth mixed with straw or rice husk. Thick walls stay cool by day and keep warmth at night, which suits the Sahel climate.
culture.a2: This architecture relies on shared upkeep: in Djenné, the community re-plasters the great mosque every year. The craft passes from mason to apprentice.

complex.label: Complex
complex.q: Why have so many African knowledge systems been underestimated?
complex.a1: Colonization often framed oral knowledge as inferior to written knowledge, which could feed an inferiority complex among heirs of these cultures.
complex.a2: Treating your language and proverbs as sources of thought restores pride without denying the world’s other knowledge traditions.

history.label: History
history.q: What does the history of the Mandinka empire tell us?
history.a1: In the 13th century, Sundiata Keita founded the Mali Empire. The Kouroukan Fouga charter, passed down orally, is said to have set rules for shared life.
history.a2: Griots (jeliw) keep genealogies and stories. They are the living memory of this history, alongside written archives.

education.label: Education
education.q: How did people study astronomy, mathematics or chemistry without modern technology?
education.a1: Through observation, memory and teaching from master to student. The sky guided farming calendars; iron forging, indigo dyeing and bogolan rely on empirical chemistry.
education.a2: In Timbuktu, thousands of manuscripts in Arabic and local languages cover science, law and religion. This scholarly tradition is documented but still partly unexplored.

travel.title: Where did the Mandé travel?
travel.intro: The Mandé did not stay in its cradle. Here are documented traces, with their limits.
travel.mapLabel: Schematic, not to scale: five places linked to the Mande world, from the Mandé in the west to Borgu and Kano in the east.

manden.text: Historic heart of the Mali Empire, founded in the 13th century.

kaabu.text: Kaabu, a federation of Mandinka kingdoms, is tied by tradition to Tiramakhan Traoré, a general of Sundiata. It became independent of Mali around 1537 and fell at Kansala in 1867.

sierra.text: Several Mande languages are spoken there (Mende, Kono, Kuranko, Susu). Their exact link to the Mali Empire is still debated.

kano.text: The Wangara, traders and scholars of Mande origin, are linked by the Kano Chronicle to the arrival of Islam, under Yaji (1349-1385) or Muhammad Rumfa (1463-1499) depending on the source.

borgou.text: The Boko and Busa speak a Mande language, and Wangara communities are documented there. The influence is commercial, religious and linguistic, not a proven conquest.

travel.caveat: Mandé does not mean the Mali Empire: Mande languages form a family much older than the empire.
travel.sources: Further reading: work on Kaabu (Canós-Donnay, Mane), the Kano Chronicle, and Brégand’s “Les Wangara du Borgou”.
